issue_paraphrase: Parsing an HTTP date from a slice of a longer header — the way a Set-Cookie header's Expires attribute is read when other attributes follow it — quietly returns null whenever the token that completes the parse happens to be the last token in the slice. The scanner correctly stops at the requested end position, but one final token is then finalized using the full string length instead, so any bytes after the end position leak into it and it stops looking like a date. A cookie whose expiry is expressed in a non-standard token order therefore loses its expiration silently: the very same date string parses fine on its own, but as a substring followed by another attribute it makes the cookie degrade to a session cookie.
fix_summary: DateFormatter.parseHttpDate(txt, start, end) now terminates its trailing token at `end` instead of `txt.length()`. Since end <= txt.length() always, the full-string overload is unaffected. Adds DateFormatterTest.testParseHttpDateSubstringDoesNotOverrunEnd asserting that the substring parse equals the isolated parse.
notes: Fast and fully offline (no network in the repro; reading the failing golden test shows the substring hypothesis directly). Build uses Maven central only; nothing on the tb21 source-repository list is pulled. issue_paraphrase: The zlib decompressor silently loses the end of a highly compressible raw-deflate stream when data is fed in chunks. Every output buffer is sized from the number of input bytes that remain, but once the inflater has pulled the last input bytes into its internal state that count drops to zero even though a large amount of decoded output is still pending; the decompressor then believes it is waiting for more input and, when the stream ends, reports that a compressed stream ended before the end-of-stream marker even though the stream was complete and valid. Payloads with extreme compression ratios — such as long runs of one repeated byte — trigger it reliably; content wrapped in gzip or zlib headers usually escapes because their trailers keep the counter above zero until the inflater finishes, which is why the standard encoders never exposed it.
fix_summary: JdkZlibDecompressor.processOutput never proposes a zero-sized output buffer anymore (floors the capacity at a new MIN_OUTPUT_BUFFER_SIZE=512) and tracks inflaterHasPendingOutput: when the last inflate() call filled the buffer completely, status() reports NEED_OUTPUT so the pending decoded data is drained before more input is requested; the flag is cleared once a call does not fill the buffer or the inflater is finished. Adds JdkZlibDecompressorTest.testHighlyCompressibleStreamIsFullyDecompressed which runs for all three wrappers and first cross-checks the compressed input with the JDK inflater.
notes: Fully offline, deterministic (in-process JDK Deflater/Inflater fixtures; no network). The regression test is parameterized over 3 ZlibWrapper values; only NONE fails at parent, so the author should assert on the whole test method (or specifically the NONE run). Module codec-compression closure: common, buffer, transport, codec-base + testsuite-common; the first reactor build absorbs ~5 min of Maven Central downloads (one-time), observed compile of the closure ~40s at -T16 on a 64-core host, per-state single-module incremental test ~5-10s at default parallelism. High compression ratio is essential to the repro: 100000 bytes of 'a' (ratio ~870:1); small payloads will not trigger it. No dependency pins needed (pure JDK java.util.zip).

issue_paraphrase: gzip streams that carry an FEXTRA extra field, as produced by BGZF and other tools that store metadata in the gzip header, cannot be decompressed: decoding throws a decompression failure and the stream is rejected, even though the same bytes decompress cleanly with the JDK's own gzip reader. The decoder reads the header's extra-field length into a value that is guaranteed to stay at its 'no extra field' sentinel by the way it is accumulated, so the extra bytes are never skipped and are handed to the inflater as if they were compressed data. Corrected handling also reads the two-byte length in the wrong byte order. Ordinary gzip output never sets this flag, which is why only unusual-but-valid producers are affected; a secondary symptom is that concatenated gzip members can contaminate each other's header parsing when the first member has an extra field.
fix_summary: JdkZlibDecoder now assembles the gzip XLEN field as a little-endian assignment ('xlen = xlen2 << 8 | xlen1;') instead of OR-ing a big-endian value into the -1 sentinel, and resets xlen to -1 when a new gzip member starts so a first-stream extra field cannot leak into the next member's header parsing. Adds JdkZlibTest.testGZIPDecodeWithExtraField and testConcatenatedGzipFirstStreamHasExtraField, which craft the FEXTRA stream by hand and sanity-check it with GZIPInputStream.
notes: Fully offline and deterministic: fixtures are hand-crafted gzip byte arrays validated with JDK GZIPInputStream inside the test; EmbeddedChannel keeps everything in-process.
